props.title: Lips of Blood

sections.content: Jean Rollin's Lips of Blood stands as one of the most haunting vampire films ever made, weaving dreamlike imagery with Gothic romance. Unlike the exploitation elements found in many of his other works like The Nude Vampire (1970) or The Shiver of the Vampires (1971), this film takes a more poetic approach. The story follows Frédéric, who becomes obsessed with a mysterious childhood memory of meeting a young woman in a ancient castle. Rollin's signature visual style - combining French New Wave influences with surrealist horror - reaches its apex here through ethereal sequences of vampires in flowing white gowns moving through Parisian ruins.

sections.content: The French horror movement of the 1970s, exemplified by films like Daughters of Darkness (1971) and The Grapes of Death (1978), merged arthouse sensibilities with Gothic horror traditions. Rollin was at the forefront, crafting atmospheric pieces that prioritized mood and visual poetry over conventional scares. His vampire films reimagined the creatures as tragic romantic figures rather than monsters, influencing later works like The Hunger (1983) and Only Lovers Left Alive (2013).

What sets Lips of Blood apart is its meditation on memory and childhood trauma. The protagonist's quest to uncover his past mirrors similar themes in Don't Look Now (1973) and Vampyr (1932), where reality and dream states blur. Rollin's use of real French locations, particularly ancient ruins and gothic architecture, grounds the supernatural elements in a tangible world while maintaining an otherworldly atmosphere. sections.content: Rollin's approach to eroticism in Lips of Blood differs significantly from his contemporaries like Jesus Franco. While films such as Vampyros Lesbos (1971) emphasized exploitation elements, Rollin treats sexuality as part of a broader artistic vision. His vampire women represent liberation rather than corruption, similar to the themes in Daughters of Darkness (1971) and later echoed in The Company of Wolves (1984).
